## Numbers you cannot feel—but labs can

<!-- lesson-illustration:body-measurement:start -->
```{=html}
<figure class="tea-lesson-figure" data-lesson-illustration="body-measurement">
  <img src="../../assets/lesson-illustrations/body-signals.svg" width="240" height="136" alt="A person beside a clock and an observation notebook." loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  <figcaption>A person, a clock and a record: measurements need a method and a time. This sketch shows no measured change.</figcaption>

```
<!-- lesson-illustration:body-measurement:end -->

Besides mood surveys, researchers can measure signals that are easy to miss in everyday life. But a useful measure is not automatically a finding about tea. This section checks what the cited experiments actually recorded.

## What the studies measured

Kimura and colleagues gave participants **200 mg of L-theanine dissolved in water** before a mental-arithmetic stress task. Compared with placebo, the L-theanine conditions showed smaller **heart-rate** and **salivary immunoglobulin A** responses. The study also recorded heart-rate variability (HRV), but its overall condition-by-time tests for the reported HRV measures were **not significant**. It does not establish that L-theanine increased HRV or improved emotional control.[^3]

Rogers and colleagues tested **250 mg caffeine**, **200 mg L-theanine**, both together, or neither in 48 adults. They measured mood, a visual-probe task, and blood pressure. Caffeine increased reported alertness and jitteriness and raised blood pressure. L-theanine moderated caffeine's blood-pressure effect, but did **not** significantly reduce jitteriness or the other reported mood effects.[^5]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: which body meters belong to these results?"}
| Measure | What it can describe | What these cited experiments show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heart rate | Beats per minute during a task | Kimura reported a smaller stress-task heart-rate response with L-theanine than with placebo.[^3] |
| HRV | Variation in time between beats | Kimura measured it, but the overall condition-by-time HRV tests were not significant.[^3] |
| Blood pressure | Pressure in the arteries | Rogers reported a caffeine increase that L-theanine moderated.[^5] |
| Skin conductance | Sweat-gland activity detectable at the skin[^1] | Neither Kimura nor Rogers reported the skin-conductance numbers previously shown here. |
| Pupil size | A possible measure of arousal | Neither cited trial establishes a caffeine-related pupil change. |

These results concern purified ingredients under specific test conditions. They do not compare an ordinary cup of brewed tea with coffee or alcohol.
:::

## Myth check: "A body meter proves how you feel"

A heart-rate change is a physiological observation, not a direct reading of calmness. Kimura's heart-rate result and Rogers's blood-pressure result answer different questions. Neither supports a precise claim about sweat spikes, pupil diameter, or better self-control from these experiments.[^3][^5]

Before accepting a body-signal headline, ask: **Which measure? Which dose? Compared with what? At what time and during which task?** The [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd) helps keep an ingredient dose separate from a brewed cup.

## A bridge into Chapter 4's protocols

The two designs show why controlled comparisons matter. Kimura used a mental-arithmetic stress task and a placebo condition; Rogers compared caffeine and L-theanine alone and together with neither ingredient.[^3][^5] Chapter 4 returns to the same habit: read the comparison and measurement before turning a result into a claim about tea.

## Story in one minute

<!-- reading-fold:start -->
:::::::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recap when you need it"}
In these cited studies, L-theanine in water reduced some responses to a stress task, and it moderated caffeine's blood-pressure effect in a separate experiment. HRV results in Kimura were not significant overall. The studies do not provide the precise pupil or skin-conductance effects previously attributed to them.
::::::::
<!-- reading-fold:end -->
::: {.callout-tip title="You can stop here"}
- Check the measure, dose, task, comparison, and timing.
- Keep a heart-rate or blood-pressure result separate from a claim that a cup of tea feels calming.
- [Return to the Chapter 2 hub](index.qmd) or [continue to Chapter 3](../module-03/index.qmd).
:::
